Headline: Candlelight vigil in Islamabad honors 10 climbers killed on Broad Peak
Body: ISLAMABAD (AP) — Mountaineers, diplomats and members of civil society gathered in Pakistan's capital Tuesday evening for a candlelight vigil honoring10 climbers killed in an avalanche on Broad Peak, as rescuers described an arduous mission to bring their fellow climbers down from one of the world's highest mountains. Rain fell as mourners lit candles and prayed for the dead, shielding the flickering flames from the downpour as they gathered on the open lawns of a sports complex in Islamabad to remember the climbers who never returned from the mountain. The vigil came days after search teams ended an operation that recovered the remains of eight climbers. Two bodies have not yet been recovered. Among the dead was renowned British-Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja. Nepal lost six climbers in the July 30 disaster, when a massive avalanche struck an international expedition. Nepal's ambassador to Pakistan, Rita Dhital, joined the vigil and paid tribute to the climbers as candles were lit in their memory. She recalled meeting Purja at her Islamabad home before the expedition and said he would often tell her, "Giving up is not in my blood." She thanked Pakistani climbers and rescuers who went onto the mountain in dangerous weather to search for the missing climbers and recover their bodies. Dhital particularly praised renowned Pakistani mountaineer Sirbaz Khan, who led the recovery team, as well as the Alpine Club of Pakistan, the military and government officials involved in the operation. The bodies of all six Nepalese climbers have been returned to their families, she said. Khan told The Associated Press that he and his team had set out hoping they would find the missing climbers alive. "I had hoped that I would hug them after finding them alive," he said. Instead, the rescuers found climbers buried beneath the avalanche. Khan said the team used shovels to dig through the snow and pull out the bodies one by one. Seeing fellow mountaineers dead on the mountain was difficult, he said, but the rescuers composed themselves and began the equally difficult task of bringing the bodies down, using ropes and makeshift stretchers. Khan said he remained deeply saddened by the deaths but took some solace in knowing that families who had waited desperately for news were able to receive the remains of their loved ones. Irfan Arshad Khan, president of the Alpine Club of Pakistan and no relation to the rescuer, said the remains of seven climbers, including all six from Nepal, had been repatriated. He saidbad weather repeatedly prevented helicoptersfrom reaching the accident site, forcing rescuers to continue much of the search and recovery operation on foot. Eight bodies were eventually brought to a location from where they could be airlifted, he said. "We have gathered here today to commemorate the passing of our great comrades," Khan told those attending the vigil. He said the days following the avalanche tested not only the endurance of those searching the mountain but also the courage of rescuers who continued on foot when helicopters could not reach them. Theinternational expedition included climbersfrom Nepal, Oman, Pakistan, China, Britain and the United States. Broad Peak, which rises 8,051 meters (26,414 feet) above sea level in the Karakoram range, is the world's 12th-highest mountain and lies near K2, the world's second-highest peak. Mountaineering accidents are common in northern Pakistan, home to some of the world's highest mountains.

Headline: Miss Universe Canada contestants apologise for wearing indigenous dress
Body: Two contestants at the Miss Universe Canada pageant have apologised after they wore attire representing indigenous culture. The incident happened during the national costume segment, when one contestant wore a fur dress and boots and another a feathered headress. "If any costume caused offence, hurt, or misunderstanding, please know that it was never our intention," the pageant said in a statement. Former winner Ashley Callingbull, a Plains Cree woman from the Enoch Cree Nation, had interrupted another part of the pageant she was co-presenting to address the issue, saying: "It's 2026, we should know better." "There was cultural appropriation that was done toward indigenous people," Callingbull said, clarifying that she wasn't there when the costumes were worn but had later seen it on a video. One of the costumes, worn by contestant Karisa Haverkamp, featured a feather headdress, an item traditionally worn by highly respected Indigenous leaders in North America. She also had a red handprint painted on her face - a symbol representing solidarity with the Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women (MMIW) movement. "I acknowledge and recognise that my outfit for the national costume caused hurt and offence to people in the indigenous community," Haverkamp wrote in an Instagram post. "I appreciate what I have learned from this experience." The other contestant, Jasleen Kaily, wore a costume with the theme "Arctic Beauty", which featured an all-fur dress and boots, known as mukluks, and two braids. Hair braiding can have deep cultural meaning for First Nations people. Kaily also apologised, saying: "My intention was never to disrespect or misrepresent indigenous culture" but rather to "recognise and celebrate one of the First Peoples of Canada". Former winner Ashley Callingbull addressed the costume controversy at the pageant's final, which she was co-hosting [Hector Vivas/Getty Images] According to the Miss Universe Canada website, the national costume segment is "a celebration of Canadian culture and heritage, combined with creativity", according to the Miss Universe Canada website. "Each delegate must showcase a unique costume, dress, or outfit inspired by Canada's traditions, symbols, and history" it states. It has now said it will introduce a "comprehensive costume guide" that will "establish clear guidelines and standards for all future pageant cycles to ensure every presentation is thoughtful and respectful". Pageant director Sonny Borrelli said he has also invited Callingbull, who is the first First Nations woman to win the competition, to be the costume segment's official liaison moving forward. He was co-presenting with Callingbull during Saturday's final, when she said the organisation's statement lacked a direct apology and invited him to address the issue. He said Miss Universe Canada takes "full responsibility" for the error. "We will learn from it, we will make it better, we will make it right," he said, Callingbull also thanked the pageant's organisers for being receptive when she reached out with concerns over the costume. "A part of reconciliation is that we educate and learn and understand and move on from these things in a good way," she said, adding: "We're going to make sure that everyone is going to be respected and honoured properly." Callingbull also spoke to CBC Indigenous about her reaction to seeing the costumes. "This cannot be real. I just couldn't get over that this was happening," she said. "Who allowed this on stage? Who approved this?" "Anything traditional or sacred should not be allowed. I was very, very upset." It is not the first time the Miss Universe Canada competition has been criticised for cultural appropriation. In 2015, the organisation said there had been a "misunderstanding" regarding entrant Paola Nunuz Valdez, who wore a totem pole costume during the national costume segment. Both she and the organisation said it had been meant to refer to her Dominican heritage. Callingbull said at the time that she had recommended Miss Universe Canada consider hiring a cultural consultant. Headline: England And Wales Ban Meta Glasses From Courtrooms
Body: Courts in England and Wales have officially banned Meta glasses,according to a report byThe Guardian. Anyone trying to enter court buildings with the glasses will have them confiscated and returned when they leave. His Majesty's Courts & Tribunals Service (HMCTS), which is responsible for all criminal, civil and family courts, is behind the decision. There's one major reason for this move, and it's the obvious one. Cameras are banned in courtrooms andMeta Glasses have cameras. Meta Glasses go a step further, as users can record footage without anyone really knowing. This means that someone could, theoretically, sit and record an entire court proceeding without anyone being the wiser. "There are clear restrictions on taking images or videos within courts and tribunals which is why the use of Meta glasses is prohibited," a spokesperson for the court toldThe Guardian. Taking images or videos in court buildings without official permission is a crime and can be prosecuted as contempt of court. The HMCTS has carved out an exception for smartphones in the courtroom, so long as they aren't used to record anything. However, it will not be making a similar exception for smart glasses. After all, one cannot surreptitiously affix a smartphone to one's face and film stuff without anyone knowing. A London court has already run into trouble with smart glasses, though not with the camera system. A man was accused earlier this year of being "assisted or coached in his replies to questions put to him during cross examination"by using smart glasses. This would've been done via built-in speakers and a connection to a nearby smartphone, though the claimant has denied the accusation. Courts on this side of the pond have also become wary of smart glasses. New York recently announced asimilar courtroom ban. This was done explicitly to prevent people from making secret recordings. It's not just courts that have rejected Meta Glasses and related smart glasses, on the grounds that they can be used tosecretly film people. Venues throughout the UKhave bannedwhat some call "pervert glasses." This includes the popular pub chain Weatherspoons, various high-end restaurants, members clubs, theaters, music venues and comic book conventions. People are buying Meta Glasses andfilming people without their consent, even posting the videos online. This is especially harrowing for women. A recent University of Sydney study found hundreds of videos on Instagram in which male "pick up artist" content creatorssecretly filmed womenand put the content online. Around 60 percent of these videos showed behavior classified as potential harassment and many of the victims were identified and doxxed. Mark Zuckerberg and his team don't seem terribly concerned about the pushback to these products. The Meta CEO was recently involved in a high-profile court trial about social media addiction and members of hisentourage were wearing the glasses. The judge had to threaten contempt of court to get them to remove the shady specs. A spokesperson for Meta toldThe Guardianthat it did not want to comment on the recent court ban. The companysold around 7 million pairsof Meta Glasses in 2025. Read more:If you're already watching YouTube daily, this subscription swap just makes sense Found this useful? Headline: Replica Christopher Columbus ship arrives in Liverpool
Body: A replica of a ship on which explorer Christopher Columbus sailed across the Atlantic 500 years ago has docked in Liverpool. The 180 tonne Nao Santa Maria will be berthed at the Royal Albert Dock for the next two weeks and is open to visitors. The vessel, with a crew of 14, is on a world tour involving 30 stops from its home port of Huelva in Spain, and aims to educate visitors about life for sailors in the 15th Century. Desiree Gonzalez, project manager on the Santa Maria, said: "Christopher Columbus's history is something that changed the world, literally, and it's an opportunity to visit while we are here in a short time, this short period of time before we go to next port." Gonzalez said sailors during Columbus's voyage in 1492, which led to Western explorers discovering the Americas, would have faced far harsher conditions than the current crew experienced. "They didn't have any bathrooms or a kitchen," she said. "They didn't have enough food, they didn't have refrigeration for their food. So, yeah, they drank a lot of wine because it didn't [go off]. "The conditions were very bad." The replica vessel is crewed by 14 people [Tom Walker/BBC] Ian Murphy, head of Liverpool's Maritime Museum, said the ship was a reminder of how daunting a voyage in the 15th Century would have been. "It was a real sort of journey into the unknown for a lot of these sailors," he said. "Out in environments with no sight of land, reliant on the skills that have been developed by seafarers for centuries before." The arrival of Europeans in the Americas led to the spread of diseases - including smallpox, influenza and measles - against which native populations had no natural defences. Estimates vary as to how much of the native population of the Americas was wiped out as a result of European settlement. They range from 50% to 95%. Columbus's arrival also allowed Europeans to establish colonies, which in turn brought about the transatlantic slave trade. Murphy also said the visit was a chance to reflect on the darker history of Columbus's voyages, which had had terrible consequences for native populations. "These ships are a symbol of that kind of European encounter with civilizations and cultures elsewhere and that's often a difficult and messy history," he said. "It's not always one of discovery. It's one of quite important impact on native cultures and native people. "It's not always an easy meeting and it's a reminder that for all we do celebrate the achievements and the skills of sailors, the impact on Indigenous peoples is often a negative one." The Santa Maria will be open for visitors until 25 August. Listen to the best ofBBC Radio Merseyside on Soundsand follow BBC Merseyside onFacebook,X, andInstagram. You can also send story ideas via Whatsapp to 0808 100 2230. Proposals could restrict visits to rubbish tips

Headline: Over 16,000 civilians detained by Russia during the war in Ukraine are still held, UN estimates
Body: UNITED NATIONS (AP) — The United Nations estimates that more than16,000 civilians detainedby Russia during itswar in Ukraineare still being "deprived of their liberty," many held incommunicado and on grounds that don't comply with international law. "Widespread and systematic torture and ill-treatment" of both Ukrainian civilian detainees and prisoners of war by Russia are continuing, includingsexual violence, said Claudia Fuentes Julio, the U.N. assistant secretary-general for human rights. She spoke at an informal meeting of the U.N. Security Council called by Latvia and the United Kingdom on Monday to spotlight the plight of civilians and soldiers taken during the war that Russia launched with a full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022. The council, which counts Russia as a permanent member, heard the accounts as both Russia and Ukraine haveescalated attacksin the four-year conflict. Since the invasion, Julio said, U.N. human rights staff have interviewed 910 Ukrainian prisoners of war and 403 civilian detainees following their release. The U.N. has not been able to visit detention facilities in Russia, and its estimated figure of those held does not break down how many are adults or children. More than 95% of theUkrainian prisoners of warand 85% of the civilian detainees reported being tortured or ill-treated, often repeatedly, the U.N. official said. They also reported sexual attacks and inhumane conditions, including food deprivation and inadequate medical services. The Geneva-based human rights office "has documented the execution of 129 Ukrainian prisoners of war at the beginning of their captivity, and the deaths of 48 Ukrainian prisoners of war in custody, resulting from torture, denial of medical care, or other inhumane conditions of detention," Julio said. The U.N. Security Council also heard emotionally wrenching accounts from Crimean Tatar human rights activist Leniie Umerova, who called herself a "political prisoner" of the Russians for almost two years, and Khuan Leyva Garsiya, a Ukrainian soldier who was among the hundreds thatheld out for months at the Azovstal steel plantin thebesieged city of Mariupolbeforeturning themselves overto the Russians in May 2022. Garsiya, who was born in Mariupol to a Ukrainian mother and Cuban father, spent 1,183 days as a POW. He said he weighed 55 kilograms (120 pounds) when he was freed, pulling out a picture of his emaciated body to show the council. He said he was tortured, beaten harder and humiliated more than other prisoners because the Russians suspected that he was a foreign mercenary due to his Cuban ancestry or an American spy because he went to college in the United States. "Russians were outraged that someone with a connection to Cuba, whom they consider an ally, would fight against their occupation army," said Garsiya, who is still in the Ukrainian military. He said the Russians tried to break the prisoners mentally and force them to confess to falsified crimes through tortures including freezing, beatings, electrocution and sexual abuse, he said. "Two of my friends were beaten to death in detention centers in the Donetsk region," Garsiya said. "Two of my friends died because of the conditions they were put in in Russian prisons and were returned in plastic bags to the homeland." For Umerova, her captivity began when she tried to enter Russia from Georgia to visit her seriously ill fatherin Crimea, which is part of Ukraine but has been occupied by Russia since 2014. She said she was placed in detention on "fabricated charges." But unlike many others, she was able to contact an attorney. In the third month, she said, her attorney obtained her release through a court order. "But as soon as the prison gates opened, a bag was put over my head and I was taken away again." In six months, she said she was moved to seven different facilities, calling it "a carousel of repression." What happened to her, Umerova said, is part of a system Russia uses to unlawfully detain, isolate, torture and fabricate charges against civilians. She named half a dozen women in Russian prisons today and said at least 84 women have faced criminal prosecution. U.N. human rights experts also interviewed 816 Russians and 57 third-country national prisoners of war from over 45 countries who were members of the Russian armed forces in Ukraine, said Julio, the assistant secretary-general. About half reported torture or ill-treatment, primarily during the initial stages of captivity and interrogation by Ukrainians, she said. But U.N. monitors reported that once they arrived in Ukrainian detention facilities, "the conditions generally comply with international humanitarian law and have improved since 2022." Russia's deputy U.N. Ambassador Maria Zabolotskaya told the council the Russian armed forces are complying with international humanitarian law, which includes the treatment of prisoners. She claimed Russian prisoners in Ukraine faced "torture and degradation, and moral and physical abuse." She called the Security Council meeting part of "a disinformation campaign against Russia," funded by NATO countries involved in the Ukraine conflict. The aim, she said, "is to derail efforts towards a peace settlement and to justify strikes on the territory of Russia and against civilians." Ukraine's deputy U.N. Ambassador Volodymyr Pavlichenko said he was struck that during Monday's meeting, Russia was not ready to discuss the return of POWs — "including their POWs" — and all civilian detainees including abducted children.

Headline: The surprising reason Prince Andrew could still receive a royal funeral despite losing his titles
Body: Despite losing his royal titles and stepping away from public life,Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, formerly Prince Andrew, is reportedly still expected to receive a ceremonial royal funeral under long-standing government contingency plans. You may also like Prince Andrew faces pivotal week as court appearance coincides with possible loss of one of his last honors Princess Eugenie breaks from family drama: Inside the home in Portugal where she welcomed her third child Princess Beatrice's husband puts marriage rift rumors to rest with a sweet birthday message Continue reading According to The Daily Mail, Andrew remains on a confidential government list of senior royals whose deaths are covered by the UK's highly classified "bridge plans," detailed operational blueprints prepared years, and sometimes decades, in advance. Queen Elizabeth II's death activated Operation London Bridge, one of the UK's secret royal funeral plans. Reports say Andrew remains covered by a similar protocol. (Mirrorpix) The publication reported that the former Duke of York has not been removed from those plans despite the dramatic changes to his royal status. The revelation has sparked renewed debate over how the monarchy and government handle ceremonial protocols for disgraced members of the Royal Family. The British government maintains confidential contingency plans for the deaths of senior members of the Royal Family. Each operation is assigned the codename of a famous bridge in the United Kingdom. King Charles stripped Andrew of his royal titles and honorary military appointments in 2025. (Justin Goff Photos) The best-known examples includeOperation London Bridge, which was activated following Queen Elizabeth II's death in 2022, andOperation Forth Bridge, the plan used after Prince Philip's death in 2021. These plans are managed by the Cabinet Office and cover everything from security and transport to media coordination, ceremonial arrangements, and preparations for visiting world leaders. Queen Elizabeth II's death in 2022 activated the government's carefully prepared Operation London Bridge funeral protocol. (Max Mumby/Indigo) According to reports, Andrew's name remains on that confidential register because the plans are administrative documents created years in advance and are not automatically revised when a royal's status changes. Reports indicate Andrew's funeral service would be held atSt. George's Chapelat Windsor Castle before he is buried at theRoyal Burial Ground at Frogmore, where many senior royals have been laid to rest since the early 20th century. The Royal Mausoleum at Frogmore is located near the Royal Burial Ground, where Prince Andrew is reportedly expected to be laid to rest under existing government plans. (Max Mumby/Indigo) While monarchs and their closest family members have traditionally been interred in the Royal Vault beneath St. George's Chapel, space has become increasingly limited, making Frogmore the resting place for many extended members of the Royal Family. Although King Charles removed Andrew's honorary military appointments and royal titles in 2025, he retained the service medals he earned during his active military career. Prince Andrew served in the Royal Navy from 1979 to 2001, including during the Falklands War. (Hulton Archive) Andrew served in the Royal Navy from 1979 to 2001, including during the Falklands War. Retired Rear Admiral Chris Parry told the Daily Mail that former Royal Navy colleagues would likely volunteer to serve as pallbearers should a ceremonial funeral take place. Andrew is said to have retained the military medals he earned during his active service. (Ken R. Goff) "The guy doesn't relinquish being a naval officer. He wasn't thrown out. He had a Falklands medal, and you can't take that away from him, and he deserves the credit for that. If somebody said to me, 'Would you do it?' I'd do it." The reports have prompted criticism because Andrew was stripped of his royal titles and public duties following years of controversy surrounding his links to Jeffrey Epstein. Prince Andrew has reportedly remained on the government's confidential royal funeral planning register. (Max Mumby/Indigo) Although ceremonial royal funerals differ from state funerals, they still require extensive government coordination, including policing, security, traffic management, and ceremonial logistics. Critics argue that any public resources devoted to such an event would likely face significant scrutiny. Reports indicate Andrew's funeral service would be held at St. George's Chapel at Windsor Castle (Max Mumby/Indigo) Neither Buckingham Palace nor the Cabinet Office has publicly commented on the reported arrangements, and the contingency plans themselves remain classified. As with other royal bridge plans, the reported protocol could still be revised in the future should the government or the monarch decide to amend it.

Headline: Europe Plunged Into Darkness With Solar Eclipse Wednesday
Body: Mainland Europe will see its first total solar eclipse in nearly 30 years on Wednesday. The rare celestial spectacle will begin in northern Russia before the moon's shadow sweeps across Greenland, Iceland, and the Atlantic, eventually reaching northern Spain and a small section of Portugal before disappearing into the Mediterranean, according toThe New York Times. Millions more across Europe, northwest Africa and parts of North America will experience a partial eclipse. The eclipse occurs when the moon passes directly between Earth and the sun. Those within the narrow path of totality will see the moon completely block the sun, revealing its corona and briefly plunging daytime skies into darkness. Most locations will experience less than two minutes of totality, according to NASA information cited by the Times. Spain is expected to be a prime viewing destination. Totality will become visible there around 8:26 p.m. local time, sweeping across the Balearic Islands before leaving land around 8:33 p.m., shortly before sunset. The Associated Press reported that the eclipse's shadow will travel about 5,130 miles, with maximum totality occurring off Iceland's western coast. Wednesday will mark mainland Spain's first total solar eclipse in more than 100 years. Anticipation has produced a rush for protective glasses across Europe. AFP reported pharmacies, opticians, and other retailers have struggled to keep certified eclipse glasses in stock. Spain's government organized the distribution of 2 million free pairs, but some locations have already exhausted supplies. Demand at Carrefour's Spanish stores reportedly increased 20-fold in recent days. Experts stress that ordinary sunglasses are not adequate protection. Looking directly at even a partially obscured sun can cause permanent eye damage. Only during totality — when the sun is completely covered — is it safe to view the eclipse without approved eye protection. Those unable to travel to the eclipse's path can still follow the event online. TheEuropean Space Agencywill broadcast live from Spain's Observatorio Astrofísico de Javalambre beginning at 7:30 p.m. Central European Summer Time. Europeans outside the path of totality will still get an impressive show. The Guardianreported London should see about 92% of the sun covered, while parts of Cornwall will reach roughly 96%. The celestial show won't end with the eclipse: The Perseid meteor shower is expected to peak overnight Wednesday into Thursday. © 2026 Newsmax. All rights reserved.

Headline: Paris tightens rules on electric scooters and other rideables
Body: Paris is cracking down on rules for users of rideables such as electric scooters, Segways, and electric skateboards, as crashes involving such devices continue to rise in the French capital. Police officers have launched a targeted operation in the city to enforce a new order for riders to wear helmets and reflective gear that took effect on 7 August. Those caught without a helmet will now be hit with a €135 fine, while riders spotted without reflective gear face a €35 fine, according to police. Hélène Denéchère, a spokesperson for the Paris police prefecture, highlighted the need for the new measures. "Since the start of the year, 136 personal injury accidents have involved vehicles of this kind, an increase of 12%. This is therefore the only category of road users in Paris for which personal injury accidents are on the rise," Denéchère said. She noted that while some riders already comply, others see the rules as an added burden. But she stressed that "wearing a helmet reduces the severity of these accidents." Public reaction in Paris remains divided, however. Rider Pierre Thoribé acknowledged the necessity of the gear despite being caught without it. "It's perfectly natural for me to have a helmet, which I don't have today… It's exceptional. I forgot my helmet," he said. Software developer Igor Monteiro, who already wears head protection, praised the enforcement. "I think it's very good. It's normal if you want safety. I've always used it... To me it's normal," he said, adding he was unaware of the new rules. Youssef Mourgui, a tattoo artist, urged fellow users to consider the risks of riding without protective gear. "Honestly, for yourself, it's good for safety. Because I know someone who works in a hospital; he told us he gets loads of people coming in, every time with their skulls smashed. There are even some now who are in wheelchairs," Mourgui said. "Not because of the police, but honestly, it's better for our health to wear a helmet." For others, the fine seems to be too hefty. One female scooter rider said the €135 fine for those caught with no helmet was in particular "a bit expensive," adding that users are getting "used to it now with everything that's going on." Those opposed to the new rules have criticised them as overly restrictive, arguing that it should be left up to personal choice. "I think it's better to let people be free and do what they want. If they have an accident afterwards, that's just tough luck for them," cyclist Romaric Bouton said. "We're not going to start holding everyone's hand and forcing them to wear a vest, a helmet, just because there are so many accidents every year. After that, we're no longer free to do what we want."

Headline: Watch: Man spins 33 hula hoops while upside down to break world record
Body: Aug. 11 (UPI) -- A Chinese man managed to spin 33 hula hoops around his body while suspended upside down to break a Guinness World Record. Yan Yanjia was suspended upside down from playground equipment in Guilin, Guangxi, and two friends then helped pull the hula hoops over his head and down to his hips. Yanjia was able to keep the hoops spinning for the time required by Guinness World Records, earning him the title for themost hula hoops spun while suspended upside down. He beat the previous record by 10 hoops. Yanjia said he started hula hooping eight years ago as a means of losing weight. "In 2018, I was diagnosed with fatty liver due to obesity, and my doctor advised me to lose weight. At that time, I bought a 2-kilogram [4.4-pound] hula hoop for exercise, and in a month, I went from 80 kg [175 pounds] to 63 kg [132 pounds]," he told Guinness World Records. "Of course, the main factor in successful fat loss is gradual control of diet." Yanjia said the next record his has his eye on involves spinning hula hoops while doing pullups. "This exercise consumes many times more force than dozens of hula hoops upside down, requiring much greater core stability," he said.

Headline: Queen Jetsun Pema of Bhutan and Princess Akiko Step Out Together for Unexpected Joint Engagement
Body: Princess Akiko of Mikasa, the second cousin of Japan'sEmperor Naruhito, is visitingBhutanthis week to mark 40 years of diplomatic relations between the two countries. King Jigme Khesar Namgyel WangchuckandQueen Jetsun Pemawelcomed Princess Akiko to Tashichhodzong, a Buddhist monastery and the seat of Bhutan's government, earlier today. Per the Bhutan royal court, Princess Akiko "was escorted to the dzong in traditional Chhipdrel procession, and received Audience with Their Majesties in the Golden Throne Room. Their Majesties and Her Imperial Highness then offered a thousand butterlamps at the Grand Kuenrey of Tashichhodzong for the victims of the earthquake that struck Kumamoto Prefecture in Japan on 28 July, and prayed for the full recovery of the affected communities." King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck and Princess Akiko.Royal Court of Bhutan After, Queen Jetsun Pema and Princess Akiko carried out a joint engagement at a traditional Japanese sweet-making workshop. Per the Queen'sofficial Facebook page, "Two chefs from Kyoto Wakuden, a renowned culinary establishment in Japan, showed Her Majesty, Her Imperial Highness, and participants from SELWA, the art of making wagashi, traditional Japanese sweets crafted to reflect the seasons and served alongside tea." Queen Jetsun Pema is the royal patron of SELWA, which works with people with disabilities "to build a more inclusive Bhutan, with better access to education, growth, and employment for all." The organization is planning to open a café to be run by youth with disabilities; the wagashi workshop "opens the door to specialised skills that can find a place in the café's offerings and similar initiatives ahead." The Bhutanese queen and the Japanese princess during the workshop.Queen Jetsun Pema/Facebook The royal women make wagashi.Queen Jetsun Pema/Facebook Princess Akiko arrived in Bhutan on August 7, and will be in the country through August 14.
